This research portfolio focuses on climate policy, climate finance, applied modelling, taxation, and sovereign incentives. The common thread is practical climate statecraft: making climate strategy operational for finance ministries, multilateral development banks, and country teams through better models, diagnostics, policy instruments, and financing structures.

# 1. Climate and Fiscal Policy: the carbon-pricing series

Carbon pricing as a finance ministry can actually use it. The series argues that production and consumption should be priced separately: production intensity with a revenue-neutral feebate, consumption with a destination-based charge, and both measured on one carbon-price-equivalent scale. Paper 1.1 sets out the architecture; the others carry the detail. Each paper comes as a short policy brief in the *Climate Fiscal Policy Briefs* series and as a longer working paper.

### 1.1 Price Production and Consumption Separately

*A two-track architecture for carbon pricing in open economies*

Carbon prices stay low in open economies because one instrument does two jobs: it pushes producers to cut emissions per unit of output, and it makes consumers pay for the carbon they use. This paper separates the jobs. A revenue-neutral feebate prices production intensity at no cost to the treasury and with a small price effect. A carbon component of VAT and forward-announced obligations on energy suppliers price consumption, imports included. A carbon-price-equivalent metric measures both. International payments above half the feebate rate make adoption a net gain, and destination-based charges turn leakage into a race to the top.

[Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.1) →](papers/Brief-OpenEconomyCarbonPricing.docx) · [Working paper →](papers/OpenEconomyCarbonPricing.docx) · [Slides →](papers/Slides-OpenEconomyCarbonPricing.pptx)

### 1.2 Feebates: The Full Carbon Price at the Margin, Without the Carbon Bill

*Decarbonizing coal-heavy power and trade-exposed industry*

Carbon taxes stall where coal dominates power or where industry competes abroad, because the tax charges producers for every tonne they still emit, not only for the tonnes they could avoid. A revenue-neutral feebate charges producers above a sector benchmark of emissions per unit of output and rebates those below it. It gives the same incentive to switch as a tax at the same rate but leaves average costs almost unchanged. Governments should use feebates where carbon taxes stall.

[Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.2) →](papers/Brief-FeebatesAndOutputBasedRebating.docx) · [Working paper →](papers/FeebatesAndOutputBasedRebating.docx) · [Slides →](papers/Slides-FeebatesAndOutputBasedRebating.pptx)

### 1.3 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment

*Carbon price recognition and scrap shuffling under the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism*

The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism cuts an importer's charge by the carbon price the exporter has effectively paid, installation by installation. Two flaws follow. Instruments that send a full price signal but pay little net, such as feebates, rebated carbon taxes and energy subsidy reform, earn no credit. And exporters can ship scrap-based steel to the EU and blast-furnace steel elsewhere, cutting reported embodied carbon with no fall in emissions. Measuring the price signal at country-sector level fixes both.

[Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.3) →](papers/Brief-IronSteelCBAM.docx) · [Working paper →](papers/IronSteelCBAM.docx) · [Slides →](papers/Slides-IronSteelCBAM.pptx)

### 1.6 Carbon Consumption Tax

*A carbon component in VAT and a forward obligation on energy suppliers*

The EU prices the carbon its factories and power plants emit but barely prices the carbon in what Europeans buy, much of it emitted abroad. A carbon component of VAT charges every good consumed in the EU, imported or domestic, for its embodied carbon while the value component of VAT falls; exports are zero-rated and imports start on generous, rebuttable default intensities. A legal obligation announced a decade ahead makes the few large suppliers of road and heating fuel pay for the carbon they sell.

[Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.6) →](papers/Brief-CarbonConsumptionTax.docx) · [Working paper →](papers/CarbonConsumptionTax.docx) · [Slides →](papers/Slides-CarbonConsumptionTax.pptx)

### 1.7 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

*The Total Effective Carbon Price: one carbon-tax equivalent for any mix of taxes, subsidies and standards*

Countries cut emissions with taxes, subsidies, standards and mandates, yet standard metrics add up explicit prices per tonne, so a clean-fuel standard or a revenue-neutral feebate scores zero. The Total Effective Carbon Price is the single economy-wide carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much as the actual policy mix, with each instrument weighted by how strongly emissions respond. Crediting, border recognition and country diagnostics can all use it.

# 2. Finance and Risk: making clean power an asset class

Clean power in developing countries is cheap to build and expensive to finance, because investors price risks the project cannot control. The series removes payment risk at its source with a payment intermediary, then turns projects into a few standard securities, each held by the investor who prices its risk most cheaply. Each paper comes as a short policy brief and a longer working paper. [Section overview →](papers/OverviewMobilisingPrivateCapital.docx)

### 2.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt

*A payment intermediary for clean power*

Solar and wind plants are cheap to build in most developing countries but expensive to finance, because lenders price the risk that a state-owned distribution company will not pay for the power. This paper proposes a payment intermediary facility that buys power under one standard contract, pays generators in full and on time whatever the distributor does, and recovers arrears itself, behind a guarantee waterfall agreed in advance. In a stylized calibration the offtaker premium adds about 11 percent to the solar tariff; guaranteeing the contract removes all of it and saves about five dollars per dollar of the guarantor's expected cost, while guaranteeing project debt saves less than it costs. India's Solar Energy Corporation shows that the design works, and its distributors' arrears show that it must come with utility reform. The state's exposure becomes smaller, contingent and contracted, but it does not vanish.

[Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 2.1) →](papers/Brief-ClimateFinanceIntermediationForCleanPower.docx) · [Working paper →](papers/ClimateFinanceIntermediationForCleanPower.docx)

### 2.2 From Projects to Asset Classes

*Two-stage finance and synthetic sovereign bonds for clean power*

Clean power projects in developing countries are financed one at a time, on bespoke terms, by investors who price construction, payment, currency and sovereign risk together. This paper splits each project at commissioning: development banks finance construction against a contingent purchase contract, and completed plants are pooled and refinanced through first-loss equity, a thin mezzanine and a senior synthetic sovereign bond co-guaranteed by highly rated sovereigns. A one-factor portfolio model shows that 5 to 10 percent subordination makes the senior bond near-AAA at plausible default correlations, and that refinancing cuts the levelized cost of solar power by about a quarter. Where there is no contract to guarantee, as for transmission, a tiered and conditional bond guarantee plays the same role.

[Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 2.2) →](papers/Brief-CleanPowerAssetClasses.docx) · [Working paper →](papers/CleanPowerAssetClasses.docx)

# 3. Sovereign Incentives: reward governments, not projects

Cutting emissions pays off globally while the costs fall on national governments, so incentives for national climate policy must come from outside, and cash transfers on the needed scale are politically impossible. The series rewards governments with cheaper borrowing instead: a guarantee is worth the full spread to the borrower but costs its provider only expected loss, so each dollar donors hold delivers several dollars of incentive. Papers 3.1 and 3.2 are the flagships. [Section overview →](papers/OverviewSovereignIncentives.docx)

### 3.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

*Notional capitalized value and guarantee-based climate incentives*

Climate finance pays countries for marginal emission cuts measured against counterfactuals nobody can observe, and pays almost nothing for carbon stocks never released. This paper proposes a notional capitalized value: a balance opened by a country's carbon stock, debited for every tonne emitted above an agreed allowance, and used not as cash but as guarantee capacity on the country's green borrowing. Because a guarantee costs its provider only expected loss and the carry on a buffer, each dollar of donor cost delivers about three dollars of incentive in a conservative case. For a stylized forest country with Guyana's carbon stock, a \$5 billion balance saves \$150 million a year and prices emissions at about \$30 per tonne. Capacity that declines as clean technology costs fall is the cheapest way to make acting now beat waiting.

[Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 3.1) →](papers/Brief-NotionalCapitalisedValueAndGuarantees.docx) · [Working paper →](papers/NotionalCapitalisedValueAndGuarantees.docx)

### 3.2 The Climate Investment Trust

*Hold capital, lend its strength*

Large international rewards for national climate policy fail because donors will not vote for cash transfers on the needed scale and governments cannot borrow against promised payments. This paper proposes a Climate Investment Trust that holds donor capital rather than spending it, and uses one pool three ways: as second-loss cover behind the guarantees that reward policy, as fee-earning co-investment in clean energy and regional first-loss funds, and as national beneficiary accounts that countries pledge as collateral now and draw only after 2050. In a stylized calibration, \$5 billion supports about \$54 billion of guarantees and delivers 2.7 to 10 dollars of interest savings per donor dollar.

[Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 3.2) →](papers/Brief-ClimateInvestmentTrust.docx) · [Working paper →](papers/ClimateInvestmentTrust.docx)

### 3.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

*Standard indicators, verification and pricing*

Sustainability-linked loans and bonds tie a government's interest rate to climate indicators, but they remain rare, bespoke and small: Uruguay's 2023 World Bank loan, the leading example, can save the country at most \$12.5 million. This paper proposes standard indicators measured as outturns, baselines set by rule, verification from published data and a published pricing schedule, with a fixed coupon for investors and the performance reward paid by a trusted intermediary. Because an interest rebate is bounded by the interest bill, the main reward should be guarantee capacity or collateral, which multiplies the incentive per dollar of funder cost several times.

[Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 3.3) →](papers/Brief-SustainabilityLinkedLending.docx) · [Working paper →](papers/SustainabilityLinkedLending.docx)


# 4. Modelling

Modelling that changes policy needs a model a finance ministry can audit. (The companion requirement, comparing instruments by what they do to emissions rather than by their headline rates, is paper 1.7 in the carbon-pricing series above.)

### 4.2 The Climate Policy Assessment Tool: Architecture, Recoding, and Fiscal Application

Policymakers need mitigation models that are detailed enough to capture sectoral policy interactions, but simple enough for real country work — and transparent enough that a finance ministry can audit what the model did. This paper sets out the core mitigation architecture of the Climate Policy Assessment Tool, with particular attention to the power sector, policy interaction, and country applications.

Three strands run through it. The first replaces CPAT's hard renewable-energy investment-flow constraint with a softer treatment based on system-adjusted marginal costs and shadow prices, representing realistic power-sector adjustment. The second reports on rebuilding the core price and demand logic as a transparent, testable kernel, using AI assistance for the translation and verification steps, and asks what that exercise implies for how policy models should be built and maintained. The third carries the output into fiscal strategy, linking long-term mitigation pathways to public and private investment, revenues, fiscal risk, and debt sustainability through a SiSePuede–CCDR–CPAT framing.

# 5. Analytics

Diagnostics built to be run by the people who hold the budget, on data they already hold.

### 5.1 Automated Excise-Fiscal Reports: Instruments, Externalities, and Policy Pathways

Finance ministries often read excise systems instrument by instrument, without seeing whether the tax system as a whole addresses externalities. This paper proposes a standardized three-part diagnostic: an excise diagnostic that categorizes each schedule line and scales rates comparably; an externality diagnostic that brings carbon, air pollution, accidents, congestion, and road damage onto a common spine; and a policy pathways section that converts findings into sequenced reform options. Sierra Leone is the worked application.
